title: III. Peasant Women Who Have Faith
paragraphs: Below, at the wooden portico built onto the outer wall of the enclosure, a crowd of about twenty peasant women had gathered. They'd been told the elder would finally be coming out, and had assembled in anticipation. Two ladies, Madame Hohlakov and her daughter, had also come out onto the portico to wait for the elder, though in a separate section set aside for women of rank.

Madame Hohlakov was a wealthy woman, still young and attractive, always dressed with taste. She was somewhat pale, with lively black eyes. She was no more than thirty-three, and had been a widow for five years. Her daughter, a girl of fourteen, was partly paralyzed. The poor child hadn't been able to walk for the past six months, and was wheeled around in a long reclining chair. She had a charming little face, thin from illness but full of good humor. There was a gleam of mischief in her big dark eyes with their long lashes. Her mother had been meaning to take her abroad since spring, but they'd been held up all summer by business connected with their estate. They'd been staying a week in our town, having come mostly on business rather than for devotion, but had already visited Father Zossima once, three days before. Though they knew the elder scarcely saw anyone now, they'd suddenly turned up again, urgently begging for “the happiness of looking once more on the great healer.”

The mother sat on a chair beside her daughter's invalid carriage, and two paces off stood an old monk—not from our monastery, but a visitor from an obscure religious house in the far north. He too had come seeking the elder's blessing.

But Father Zossima, on entering the portico, went first straight to the peasants crowded at the foot of the three steps leading up into it. He stood on the top step, put on his stole, and began blessing the women pressing around him. One deranged woman was led up to him. The moment she caught sight of the elder she began shrieking and writhing as though in labor. Laying the stole on her forehead, he read a short prayer over her, and she was at once calmed and quieted.

I don't know how it is now, but in my childhood I often saw and heard these “possessed” women in the villages and monasteries. They'd be brought to mass, and would squeal and bark like dogs, loud enough to be heard through the whole church. But the moment the sacrament was carried in and they were led up to it, the “possession” would stop at once, and the sick women would always be soothed for a while. As a child I found this deeply striking and astonishing, but I heard from country neighbors and from my town teachers that the whole illness was faked to get out of work, and that it could always be cured with a bit of proper strictness; various anecdotes were told to back this up. But later on I learned, to my surprise, from medical specialists that there's nothing fake about it, that it's a terrible illness women are subject to, especially common here in Russia, and that it comes from the hard lot of peasant women. It's a disease, I was told, arising from exhausting labor taken up too soon after difficult, unassisted childbirths, and from the hopeless misery, the beatings, and so on, which some women simply couldn't bear as well as others could. The strange, instant healing of the frantic, struggling woman the moment she was brought before the holy sacrament, which had been explained to me as a matter of malingering and clerical trickery, most likely arose in the most natural way possible. Both the women supporting her and the invalid herself believed, without question, as an absolute truth, that the evil spirit possessing her couldn't hold out if the sick woman were brought to the sacrament and made to bow down before it. And so, in a nervous, psychologically disturbed woman, a kind of convulsion of the whole body would take place—and was bound to take place—at the moment of bowing down before the sacrament, stirred up by the expectation of a miraculous cure and the absolute belief that it would happen; and it did happen, though only for a moment. It was exactly the same now, the instant the elder touched the sick woman with his stole.
Many of the women in the crowd were moved to tears of rapture by the moment; some strained to kiss the hem of his robe, others cried out in a kind of sing-song wail.
He blessed them all and spoke with some of them. He already knew the “possessed” woman. She came from a village only four miles from the monastery, and had been brought to him before.

“But here's one from far away.” He pointed to a woman, not old, but very thin and worn, her face not just sunburnt but nearly blackened by exposure. She was on her knees, gazing at the elder with a fixed stare—there was something almost frenzied in her eyes.

“From far away, Father, from far away! From two hundred miles off. From far away, Father, from far away!” the woman began in a sing-song voice, as if chanting a dirge, swaying her head from side to side, her cheek resting in her hand.

There's a silent, long-suffering grief you find among the peasantry. It draws inward and stays still. But there's also a grief that breaks loose, and from that moment bursts into tears and finds its outlet in wailing. This is especially common among women. But it's no lighter a grief than the silent kind. Wailing brings comfort only by tearing the heart open further still. Grief of that kind doesn't want to be consoled. It feeds on the very sense of its own hopelessness. The wailing springs only from a constant craving to reopen the wound.
“You're of the tradesman class?” said Father Zossima, looking at her curiously.

“Townsfolk we are, Father, townsfolk. Though we're peasants at heart even living in town. I've come to see you, oh Father! We heard about you, Father, we heard about you. I've buried my little son, and I've come on a pilgrimage. I've been to three monasteries, but they told me, 'Go, Nastasya, go to him'—meaning you. I've come; I was at the service yesterday, and today I've come to you.”
“What are you weeping for?”

“It's my little son I'm grieving for, Father. He was three years old—three years all but three months. I'm in agony over my boy, Father, over my little boy. He was the last one I had left. There were four of us, my Nikita and I, and now we've no children—our dear ones are all gone. I buried the first three without grieving so terribly, but this last one I can't forget. He's always standing before me. He never leaves me. He's withered my heart. I look at his little clothes, his little shirt, his little boots, and I wail. I lay out everything that's left of him, all his little things. I look at them and wail. I say to Nikita, my husband, 'Let me go on a pilgrimage, master.' He's a driver. We're not poor people, Father, not poor—he drives his own horse. It's all ours, the horse and the carriage. And what good is any of it to us now? My Nikita's taken to drinking while I'm away. He's sure to. It's always been that way before. The moment I turn my back he gives in to it. But now I don't think about him at all. It's three months since I left home. I've forgotten him. I've forgotten everything. I don't want to remember. And what would our life together even be now? I'm done with him, I'm done. I'm done with all of them. I don't want to look at my house or my belongings. I don't want to see anything at all!”

“Listen, mother,” said the elder. “Once, in olden times, a holy saint saw in the Temple a mother like you, weeping for her little one, her only child, whom God had taken. 'Knowest thou not,' the saint said to her, 'how bold these little ones are before the throne of God? Truly, there are none bolder than they in the Kingdom of Heaven. “Thou didst give us life, O Lord,” they say, “and scarcely had we looked upon it when Thou didst take it back again.” And they ask, and ask so boldly, that God gives them at once the rank of angels.' 'Therefore,' the saint said, 'thou too, O mother, rejoice and weep not, for thy little son is with the Lord, among the fellowship of angels.' That's what the saint said to the weeping mother, long ago. He was a great saint, and he wouldn't have spoken falsely. So you too, mother, know that your little one is surely standing before the throne of God, rejoicing, happy, and praying to God for you—so weep not, but rejoice.”
The woman listened to him, her cheek still in her hand, eyes lowered. She sighed deeply.

“My Nikita tried to comfort me with those same words. 'Foolish woman,' he said, 'why do you weep? Our son is surely singing with the angels before God.' He says that to me, but he weeps himself. I see him cry, same as me. 'I know, Nikita,' I say. 'Where else could he be, if not with the Lord God? Only, here with us, he isn't as he used to be, sitting beside us the way he used to.' And if only I could look at him one little time—if only I could peek at him for one little moment, without going up to him, without speaking, if I could just hide in a corner and see him for one little minute, hear him playing in the yard, calling out in his little voice, 'Mammy, where are you?' If only I could hear him pattering with his little feet across the room just once, only once—because so often, so often, I remember how he used to run to me, shouting and laughing—if I could only hear his little feet I'd know it was him! But he's gone, Father, he's gone, and I'll never hear him again. Here's his little sash, but him I'll never see or hear now.”

She pulled out from inside her dress her boy's little embroidered sash, and the moment she looked at it she began shaking with sobs, covering her eyes with her fingers as the tears poured through them in a sudden stream.

“This is Rachel of old,” said the elder, “weeping for her children, and refusing comfort because they are no more. That is the fate set on earth for mothers like you. Do not be comforted. Comfort isn't what you need. Weep, and do not be consoled—only weep. Just remember, every time you weep, that your little son is one of the angels of God now, that he looks down at you from there and sees you, and rejoices in your tears, and points them out to the Lord God; and for a long while yet you'll carry this great mother's grief. But in the end it will turn into quiet joy, and your bitter tears will become only tears of tender sorrow, the kind that purifies the heart and frees it from sin. And I'll pray for the peace of your child's soul. What was his name?”
“Alexey, Father.”
“A sweet name. After Alexey, the man of God?”
“Yes, Father.”

“What a saint he was! I'll remember him, mother, and your grief, in my prayers—and I'll pray for your husband's health too. It's a sin for you to leave him. Your little one will see from heaven that you've abandoned his father, and he'll weep over you. Why trouble his happiness? He is alive—for the soul lives forever—and though he's not in the house, he's near you, unseen. How could he come into the house if you say the house is hateful to you? Who would he go to, if he can't find his father and mother together? He comes to you in dreams now, and you grieve. But then he'll send you gentle dreams instead. Go to your husband, mother; go this very day.”

“I'll go, Father, at your word. I'll go. You've gone straight to my heart. My Nikita, my Nikita, you're waiting for me,” the woman began in her sing-song voice; but the elder had already turned away, to a very old woman dressed like a town-dweller, not a pilgrim. Her eyes showed she'd come with a purpose, to say something in particular. She said she was the widow of a non-commissioned officer, and lived close by in town. Her son Vasenka was in the commissariat service, and had gone off to Irkutsk in Siberia. He'd written twice from there, but now a year had passed without a letter. She'd tried to make inquiries about him, but didn't know the right place to ask.

“Just the other day Stepanida Ilyinishna—she's a rich merchant's wife—said to me, 'You go, Prohorovna, and have your son's name put down for prayer at church, and pray for the peace of his soul as if he were dead. His soul will be troubled,' she said, 'and he'll write you a letter.' And Stepanida Ilyinishna told me it was a sure thing, tried many times before. Only I'm not certain… Oh, you, our light—is it true, or false, and would it even be right to do?”

“Don't even think of it. It's shameful to ask such a question. How could one possibly pray for the peace of a living soul? And his own mother, at that! It's a great sin, close to sorcery. It's only forgiven you because of your ignorance. Better to pray to the Queen of Heaven, our swift defender and helper, for his good health, and to ask her forgiveness for your error. And I'll tell you one more thing, Prohorovna: either your son will come back to you soon, or he'll be sure to send a letter. Go, and be at peace from now on. Your son is alive, I tell you.”
“Dear Father, God reward you, our benefactor, who prays for all of us and for our sins!”

But the elder had already noticed, in the crowd, two burning eyes fixed on him. An exhausted, consumptive-looking, though still young peasant woman was gazing at him in silence. Her eyes pleaded, but she seemed afraid to come closer.
“What is it, my child?”
“Absolve my soul, Father,” she said softly, and slowly sank to her knees and bowed down at his feet. “I have sinned, Father. I am afraid of my sin.”
The elder sat down on the lower step. The woman crept closer to him, still on her knees.

“I have been a widow these three years,” she began in a half-whisper, with a kind of shudder. “My life with my husband was hard. He was an old man. He used to beat me cruelly. He fell ill; I looked at him and thought, if he got well, if he got up again, what then? And then the thought came to me—”
“Wait!” said the elder, and he brought his ear close to her lips.
The woman went on in a low whisper, so faint it was almost impossible to make out. She finished quickly.
“Three years ago?” asked the elder.
“Three years. At first I didn't think much about it, but now I've started to fall ill, and the thought won't leave me.”
“Have you come a long way?”
“Over three hundred miles.”
“Have you confessed it?”
“I have confessed it. Twice I've confessed it.”
“Have you been admitted to Communion?”
“Yes. I am afraid. I am afraid to die.”

“Fear nothing, and never be afraid; and don't fret. As long as your repentance doesn't fail, God will forgive everything. There is no sin, and there can be no sin on the whole earth, that the Lord will not forgive to the truly repentant! A man cannot commit a sin so great it would exhaust the infinite love of God. Can there even be a sin that could outstrip the love of God? Think only of repentance, of continual repentance—but let go of fear entirely. Believe that God loves you in a way you can't even conceive; that he loves you with your sin, in your sin. It's been said, of old, that there's more joy in heaven over one repentant sinner than over ten righteous men. Go, and be not afraid. Don't turn bitter against people. Don't be angry when you're wronged. Forgive the dead man in your heart whatever wrong he did you. Be reconciled with him, truly. If you repent, you love. And if you love, you belong to God. All things are atoned for, all things are saved, by love. If I, a sinner just as you are, can be tender with you and pity you, how much more will God. Love is such a priceless treasure that you can redeem the whole world with it, and atone not only for your own sins, but for the sins of others too.”
He made the sign of the cross over her three times, took a small icon from around his own neck, and put it on her. She bowed all the way to the ground without a word.
He stood up, and looked cheerfully at a healthy peasant woman holding a tiny baby.
“From Vyshegorye, dear Father.”
“Five miles you've dragged yourself with the baby. What do you need?”

“I came to look at you. I've been to see you before—or have you forgotten? You've no great memory if you've forgotten me. They told us you were ill. Thinks I, I'll go see for myself. Well, now I see you, and you're not ill at all! You'll live another twenty years. God bless you! There's plenty praying for you—how could you fall ill?”
“Thank you for all of it, daughter.”

“By the way, I've got one thing to ask, not a big one. Here's sixty kopecks. Give it, dear Father, to someone poorer than me. I thought, as I was coming along, better to give it through you. You'll know who to give it to.”
“Thank you, my dear, thank you! You're a good woman. I love you. I'll certainly see to it. Is that your little girl?”
“My little girl, Father, Lizaveta.”
“May the Lord bless you both, you and your little Lizaveta! You've gladdened my heart, mother. Farewell, dear children, farewell, dear ones.”
He blessed them all and bowed low to them.
